questions.solution:
$ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$

$a, b, c \in { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }$

$n ( s ) = 6 \times 6 \times 6 = 216$

For equal~root~$D = 0$

$⇒ b^{2} = 4ac$

Case I:~$ac = 1$

\left(a, b, c\right) = \left(1, 2, 1\right)$

Case II:~$ac = 4$

\left($a, b, c\right) = \left($1, 4, 4\right)$

questions.q: If $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A \cap B)=0.1$, and $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ are the roots of the equation $12 x^2-7 x+1=0$, then the value of $\frac{\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{A}} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}})}{\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{A}} \cap \overline{\mathrm{B}})}$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$P(A \cap B)=0.1, P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ are the roots of the equation $12 x^2-7 x+1=0\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad P(A \mid B) P(B \mid A)=\frac{1}{12} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \times \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}=\frac{1}{12} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad P(A) P(B)=12(0.1)^2 \\
& =0.12
\end{aligned}$ Also, $P(A \mid B)+P(B \mid A)=\frac{7}{12}\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & P(A \cap B)\left(\frac{1}{P(B)}+\frac{1}{P(A)}\right)=\frac{7}{12} \\
\Rightarrow & P(A)+P(B)=\frac{7}{12} \times \frac{0.12}{0.1} \\
\Rightarrow & P(A)+P(B)=0.7 \\
& \frac{P(\bar{A} \cup \bar{B})}{P(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B})}=\frac{P(\overline{A \cap B})}{P(\overline{A U B})} \\
& =\frac{1-P(A \cap B)}{1-P(A \cup B)} \\
& =\frac{1-0.1}{1-(0.7-0.1)}=\frac{0.9}{0.4}=\frac{9}{4}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A six faced die is biased such that $3 \times P$(a prime number)$= 6 \times P$(a composite number)$= 2 \times P  \left(1\right)$. Let $X$ be a random variable that counts the number of times one gets a perfect square on some throws of this die. If the die is thrown twice, then the mean of $X is$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let& $\dfrac{P\left(\text{a prime number}\right)}{2} = \dfrac{P\left(\text{a composite number}\right)}{1} = \dfrac{P\left(1\right)}{3} = k$

So,~$P$(a prime number)$= 2k$,

$P$~(a composite number)$= k$,

and~$P\left(1\right) = 3k$

i.e.~$6k + 2k + 3k = 1$

$⇒ k = \dfrac{1}{11}$

$P ( \text{success} ) = P\left(1\text{or}4\right) = 3k + k = \dfrac{4}{11}$

Number of trials,~$n = 2$

$∴$~required mean$= np = 2 \times \dfrac{4}{11} = \dfrac{8}{11}$

questions.q: Bag$A$ contains $3$ white, $7$ red balls and bag $B$ contains $3$ white, $2$ red balls. One bag is selected at random and a ball is drawn from it. The probability of drawing the ball from the bag $A$, if the ball drawn in white, is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: Given balls in bags are $A \to 3W, 7R$, $B \to 3W, 2R$

Let, ${E}_{1}: A$ is selected

, ${E}_{2}: B$ is selected

and $E$: white ball is drawn

Using Baye's theorem,
$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{E1}{E}\right) = \dfrac{P ( {E}_{1} ) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{E1}\right)}{P\left({E}_{1}\right) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{E1}\right) + P\left({E}_{2}\right) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{E2}\right)}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{E1}{E}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{10}}{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{5}}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{E1}{E}\right) = \dfrac{320}{\dfrac{3}{20} + \dfrac{6}{20}}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{E1}{E}\right) = \dfrac{3}{3 + 6}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{E1}{E}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
It is given that& $P ( H ) = 3P ( T )$

$∴ P ( H ) = \dfrac{3}{4}, P ( T ) = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Since coin is tossed till either~$1H$~or $3T$~occurs. So, process will end in the maximum of~$3$~throws.

$Xi$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$P \left(Xi\right)$ \dfrac{3}{4} \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{3}{4}

Now we know that,

Mean is given by~$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{X}_{i}P \left({X}_{i}\right)~

Mean$= 1 $\times $\dfrac{3}{4} +2 $\times $\dfrac{3}{16} +3 $\times $\dfrac{1}{16}= \dfrac{21}{16}$

Hence, this is the correct option.

$

questions.q: Out of 11 consecutive natural number if three numbers are selected at random (without repetition), then the probability that they are in A.P. with positive common difference is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$2b = a + c ⇒$sum of~$a\text{ \text{ and } }c$~is even and~$b$~depends on~$a\text{ \text{ and } }c$

Thus, we can not choose all three independently, but we can~choose $a\text{ \text{ and } }c$

Moreover,~$a\text{and}c$ should be~both~either even or odd as their sum is even.

Out of $11$~consecutive natural numbers, either~five~are~even and six are~odd or~six are& even and five are odd.

Hence,& $P = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{C2 5 + C2 6}{C3 11} + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{C2 6 + C2 5}{C3 11} = \dfrac{5}{33}$

questions.q: Box $1$~contains~$30$~cards numbered $1$ to~$30$~and Box $2$ contains~$20$~cards numbered~$31$~to~$50$. A box is selected at random and a card is drawn from it. The number on the card is found to be a non-prime number. The probability that the card was drawn from Box~$1$ is&
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$P \left({B}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} =P \left({B}_{2}\right)

Box~${B}_{1}$~have~$20$~non-prime numbers~\left$\{1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30\right\}$

$⇒ $P\left($NP / {B}_{1}\right) = $\dfrac{20}{30}

Box~${B}_{1}$~have~$15$~non-prime numbers~\left$\{32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 38, 39, 40, 42, 44, 45, 46, 48, 49, 50\right\}$

$⇒ P \left($NP / {B}_{2}\right) = $\dfrac{15}{20}

Probability of non-prime$= P\left($NP\right)$.

$P\left($NP\right) = P \left({B}_{1}\right) . P \left(NP / {B}_{1}\right) + P\left({B}_{2}\right) .P\left(NP / {B}_{2}\right)$

$= $\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{20}{30} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{15}{20}

$P\left({B}_{1}/ NP\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{20}{30}}{\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{20}{30} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{15}{20}} = \dfrac{8}{17}$

questions.q: The probability that a relation $R$ from \left\{x, y\right\}$ to \left\{x, y\right\}$ is both symmetric and transitive, is equal to:

questions.solution:
Total number of elements in the Cartesian product will be& $4$, so total possible relations will be~${2}^{4} = 16$

The relations which will be symmetric and transitive both will be~\left\{\right\}, \left\{x, x\right\}, \left\{y, y\right\}, \left\{\left(x, x\right), \left(y, y\right)\right\}, \left\{\left(x, x\right), \left(x, y\right), \left(y, x\right)\left(y, y\right)\right\}$

~i.e.~$5$~relations

Hence, required probability will be~$\dfrac{5}{16}$

questions.q: Two integers are selected at random from the set $\{1,2, \ldots, 11\}$. Given that the sum of selected numbers is even, the conditional probability that both the numbers are even is :

questions.q: Three rotten apples are accidently mixed with fifteen good apples. Assuming the random variable $x$ to be the number of rotten apples in a draw of two apples, the variance of $x$ is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given apples are: $3$ bad, $15$ good

Let $X$ be no. of bad apples.

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{{}^{15}{C}_{2}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{15 !}{2 ! \times 13 !}}{\dfrac{18 !}{2 ! \times 16 !}}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{15 \times 14}{18 \times 17} = \dfrac{5 \times 7}{3 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{35}{51}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 1\right) = \dfrac{{}^{3}{C}_{1}{×}^{15}{C}_{1}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{3 \times 15}{9 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 1\right) = \dfrac{5}{17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 2\right) = \dfrac{{}^{3}{C}_{2}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{3}{9 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 2\right) = \dfrac{3}{153}$

$⇒ E\left(X\right) = 0 \times \dfrac{35}{51} + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{17} + 2 \times \dfrac{3}{153}$

$⇒ E\left(X\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

We know that, $Var\left(X\right) = E\left(X^{2}\right) - \left(E\left(X\right)\right)2$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = 0 \times \dfrac{35}{51} + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{17} + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{51} - \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)2$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = \dfrac{19}{51} - \dfrac{1}{9}$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = \dfrac{40}{153}$

questions.q:
Let $A$ and $B$~be two events such that $P\left(B ∣ A\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}$, $P\left(A ∣ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{7}$ and $P\left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{9}$. Consider~

\left(S1\right)P\left(A^{'} ∪ B\right) = \dfrac{5}{6}$,

~\left(S2\right)P\left(A^{'} ∩ B^{'}\right) = \dfrac{1}{18}$. Then
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

& $A$ and $B$~be two events such that $P\left(B ∣ A\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}$, $P\left(A ∣ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{7}$ and $P\left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{9}$,~

Now using the formula of conditional probability we get,

$P\left(A ∣ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{7} ⇒ \dfrac{P\left(A ∩ B\right)}{P\left(B\right)} = \dfrac{1}{7}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{9}}{P\left(B\right)} = \dfrac{1}{7}$

$⇒ P\left(B\right) = \dfrac{7}{9}$

Now again using formula we get,

$P\left(B ∣ A\right) = \dfrac{2}{5} ⇒ \dfrac{P\left(A ∩ B\right)}{P\left(A\right)} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{9}}{P\left(A\right)} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{5}{18}$

Now we know that,

~$P \left(A^{'} ∪ B\right) = 1 - P \left($A ∪ B\right) + $P\left($B\right)$

$⇒ $P\left($A^{'} ∪ B\right) = 1 - $P\left($A\right) + P \left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{5}{6}$

And~$P\left(A^{'} ∩ B^{'}\right) = 1 - P\left(A ∪ B\right)$~

{also $P \left(A ∪ B\right) = P \left($A\right) + $P\left($B\right) - $P\left($A ∩ B\right)}

$⇒ $P\left($A^{'} ∩ B^{'}\right) = 1 - P \left(A\right) - P \left(B\right) + P \left($A ∩ B\right) = $\dfrac{1}{18}

$⇒$ Both \left($S1\right)$ and \left(S2\right)$ are true.

$

Now we will find~$P \left(\overset{¯}{A}\right)~or possibilities for~$| M | = 0$

So, for~$| M | = 0$~cases will be,

1.\left[\begin{cases}$1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{cases}\right]$ or \left[\begin{cases}$0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{cases}\right]$ or \left[\begin{cases}$2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{cases}\right] \to$ Total matrix $= 3$
2. Two $1 ' s$ and Two $0 ' s\to$ Total matrix $= 4$
3. Two $2 ' s$ and Two $0 ' s\to$ Total matrix $= 4$
4. Two $1 ' s$ and Two $2 ' s\to$ Total matrix$= 4$
5. One $1$ and three $0 ' s\to$ Total matrix $= 4$
6. One $2$ and Three $0 ' s\to$ Total matrix $= 4$
7. One $1$ and one $2$ and two $0 ' s\to$ Total matrix $= 8$

So, total cases for which~\left|$M\right| = 0$~is~$31$,

So probability will be~$P\left(\overset{¯}{A}\right) = \dfrac{31}{81}
Hence,~$P ( A ) = 1 - \dfrac{31}{81} = \dfrac{50}{81}$

questions.q: A coin is tossed three times. Let $X$ denote the number of times a tail follows a head. If $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ denote the mean and variance of $X$, then the value of 64 \left(\mu+\sigma^2\right) is :

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given that variance of& $\alpha - \beta$~is~$\dfrac{p}{q}$

$\alpha \in \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$

$\beta \in \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 0$~($6$ case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = - 1$~($5$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = - 2$~($4$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = - 3$~($3$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = - 4$~($2$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = - 5$~($1$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 1$~($5$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 2$~($4$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 3$~($3$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 4$~($2$~case)

\left(\alpha - \beta\right) = 5$~($1$~case)

Mean~$= 0$

We know that variance~$= \dfrac{\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{f}_{i}\left({x}_{i} - x\right)2}{\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{f}_{i}}$

Variance$= {σ}^{2} = \dfrac{{0}^{2} \times 6 + 2 \times {1}^{2} \times 5 + 2 \times {2}^{2} \times 4 + 2 \times {3}^{2} \times 3 + 2 \times {4}^{2} \times 2 \times {5}^{2} \times 1}{36}$

$= \dfrac{2}{36} \times \left(5 + 16 + 27 + 32 + 25\right) = \dfrac{105}{18} = \dfrac{35}{6}$

$∴ p = 35$

Sum of divisors of $p = 1 + 5 + 7 + 35 = 48$

Option \left(3\right) is correct.

$

questions.q: If the numbers appeared on the two throws of a fair six faced die are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then the probability that $x^{2} + \alphax + \beta > 0$, for all $x \in R$, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Total sample space of two dice will be equal to& $6 \times 6 = 36$

Now for~$x^{2} + \alphax + \beta > 0$~its discriminant~$D$~must be less than zero,

So~$D = b^{2} - 4ac < 0$~or~${α}^{2} - 4\beta < 0⇒ {α}^{2} < 4\beta$~

Now, if $\alpha = 1, \beta$ can take values $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$

If $\alpha = 2, \beta$ can take values $2, 3, 4, 5, 6$

If $\alpha = 3, \beta$ can take values $3, 4, 5, 6$

If $\alpha = 4, \beta$ can take values $5, 6$

If $\alpha = 5$~and $6$, no value of $\beta$ possible

So number of favourable ways $= 17$

Required probability$= \dfrac{favourable ways}{total sample space}= \dfrac{17}{36}$

Let $b=1 \Rightarrow 1-4 a c \geq 0$ (Not feasible) $\begin{aligned} & b=2 \Rightarrow 4-4 a c \geq 0 \\ & 1 \geq a c \Rightarrow a=1, c=1, \\ & b=3 \Rightarrow 9-4 a c \geq 0 \\ & \frac{9}{4} \geq a c \\ & \Rightarrow a=1, c=1 \\ & \Rightarrow a=1, c=2 \\ & \Rightarrow a=2, c=1 \\ & b=4 \Rightarrow 16-4 a c \geq 0 \\ & 4 \geq a c\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow a=1, c=1 \\ & \Rightarrow a=1, c=2 \quad \Rightarrow a=2, c=1 \\ & \Rightarrow a=1, c=3 \quad \Rightarrow a=3, c=1 \\ & \Rightarrow a=1, c=4 \quad \Rightarrow a=4, c=1 \\ & \Rightarrow a=2, c=2 \\ & \text { Probability }=\frac{12}{(4)(4)(4)}=\frac{3}{16}=\frac{m}{m} \\ & m+n=19\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Four fair dice are thrown independently 27 times. Then the expected number of times, at least two dice show up a three or a five, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
There are only two outcomes, success which stands for getting either 3 or 5, and failure, stands for getting any other outcome.

Probability for success$= p = \dfrac{2}{6}$

Probability for failure$= q = \dfrac{4}{6}$

Number of trials$= n = 27$

Number of dice$= 4$

Using Binomial Probability,

P(at least 2 shows 3 or 5)~$= C2 4 \cdot \left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)2\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right)2 + C3 4 \left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)3\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right) + C4 4 \left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)4$

$= \dfrac{384 + 128 + 16}{64} = \dfrac{11}{27}$

Expectation is numerically same as mean.

$∴$ expectation$= np$

$= 27 \cdot \dfrac{11}{27} = 11$

questions.q: If the probability that a randomly chosen $6$-digit number formed by using digits~$1$ and~$8$ only is a multiple of~$21$ is $p$, then $96p$& is equal to _____.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We have to choose& $6$~digit number by using~$1 \text{ and } 8$~and it must be divisible by 21,

So, equal number of digits~$1$~and~$8$~should be used~to form a number divisible by~$3$~and $7$. (Or all the digits are either $1$~or~$8$)

In all cases whatever number is formed using six~${1}^{'}$~or six~${8}^{'}$s or three~${1}^{'}$s~$+$~three~${8}^{'}$s, that number can be splited into sum of multiples of~$1001, 1008, 8001, 8008$~(all of them are divisible by $7$). So, all the numbers thus formed will be divisible by~$21$,

Example:~$811188 = 8001 \times {10}^{2} + 1008 \times 10 + 1008$

Number of such numbers~$= \dfrac{6 !}{3 ! 3 !} + 2 = 22$

Required Probability,~$p = \dfrac{22}{26} = \dfrac{11}{32}$

$∴ 96p = \dfrac{11}{22} \times 96 = 33$
